statement: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. A path 1 m wide runs all the way round the inside edge of the garden. What is the area of the path, in square metres?

choices.misconception: I took only 1 m off each side length, so I used an inside part of 11 m by 6 m and got 84 - 66.
I made all four strips of path 2 m shorter, 10 + 10 + 5 + 5, so the corner squares were not counted at all.
I multiplied the distance round the garden, 38 m, by the width of 1 m, so each corner square was counted twice.
I worked out the area of the part inside the path, 10 m by 5 m, instead of the area of the path itself.

hints: Sketch the garden and shade the path along all four edges.
Find the area of the whole garden and the area of the part inside the path, then subtract. Check on your sketch how much the path takes off each side.
The whole garden is 12 x 7 = 84 square metres. The path takes 1 m off both ends of each side, so the inside part is 10 m by 5 m.

solutions.reliable: The whole garden is 12 x 7 = 84 square metres. The path is 1 m wide on every side, so the part inside it loses 1 m at both ends of its length and of its width: it is 10 m by 5 m, which is 50 square metres. The path is 84 - 50 = 34 square metres. The transferable idea: a sketch shows that a border eats into both ends of every side, which is exactly where the corner squares hide.
solutions.elegant: Cut the path into two long strips 12 m by 1 m and two short strips that fit between them, 5 m by 1 m. Each corner square now belongs to one strip only, so the area is 12 + 12 + 5 + 5 = 34 square metres.

whyOnTest: Drawing the path shows its four corner squares, which get counted twice or not at all by anyone who works from the words alone.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
